Patient Case Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 68-year-old widowed African man, a former professional dancer and current dance instructor, who presents for an initial evaluation. He is tall and lean, with a dancer's posture, but today he sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped tightly in his lap. He speaks in a low, measured voice, often pausing to look at the floor before continuing. He describes himself as a man who has "always moved through life," but now feels "frozen."

The traumatic event occurred fourteen months ago. Mr. A. was driving home from a late rehearsal at the community center where he teaches. It was a rainy night, and he was listening to an old recording of a performance he had choreographed for his late wife, a pianist. He recalls a moment of distraction-hearing her voice in the music-and then a blinding flash of headlights. A pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on the driver's side. He remembers the sound of twisting metal, the sensation of being thrown sideways, and the shattering glass. He was trapped in the vehicle for nearly forty minutes. He did not lose consciousness, and he vividly recalls the smell of gasoline and the feeling of his own blood, warm and wet, running down his face. He remembers thinking, clearly and calmly, "This is it. This is how I die."

Physically, he recovered. He had a broken collarbone, three cracked ribs, and deep lacerations to his left arm. The physical therapy was difficult, but he is a disciplined man. He was back to teaching basic dance steps within four months. But the world, he says, no longer feels solid.

The most immediate and pervasive change is his relationship to driving. He has not driven a car since the accident. He sold his vehicle, a loss he feels keenly, as it was the car he and his wife used for weekend trips to the coast. Now, he relies on his adult daughter to drive him to the studio, or he takes the bus. The bus is a torment. Every sudden stop, every honk from another driver, sends a jolt of pure panic through his body. He will break into a cold sweat, his heart hammering so hard he feels he might faint. He has learned to sit near the back door so he can escape quickly if he needs to.

The intrusive memories are relentless. They are not just thoughts; they are full sensory replays. The screech of tires on pavement, the smell of burnt rubber or gasoline, the sound of a car door slamming too hard-any of these can trigger a flashback. During his dance classes, he is fine as long as he is moving. But when he is demonstrating a slow, sustained movement, or when the music is quiet and he hears a car pass by the open window, he will freeze mid-gesture. His students have learned to wait. He cannot explain it to them. He feels a deep, visceral shame, as if his body is betraying the very discipline he built his life around.

He avoids more than just driving. He has stopped going to the grocery store because the parking lot is too open, too full of moving vehicles. He has stopped attending the community music nights he used to love, because the walk from the parking lot to the building feels like running a gauntlet. His social world has shrunk to the dance studio and his daughter's living room. He describes a constant, low-grade state of hypervigilance. He scans the horizon for threats. He cannot sit with his back to a door.

Sleep is a battleground. He dreads the night. He has vivid, terrifying nightmares of the crash-the same scene, over and over. He often wakes up in a panic, his body drenched in sweat, convinced he is still in the car. He has taken to sleeping in a recliner in his living room, as the sensation of lying flat in a bed feels too much like being trapped in the wreckage.

He describes a profound emotional numbness. "I used to feel the music," he says, his voice cracking for the first time. "Now I just hear it." He cannot cry. He cannot feel joy when his students master a difficult step. He feels detached from his own life, as if he is watching himself from a great distance. The loss of his wife, who died five years ago, feels newly raw, as if the accident tore open a wound that had begun to heal. He feels guilty for surviving, guilty for the burden he places on his daughter, and guilty for the fear that has stolen his dancer's grace. He is a man who has always moved forward, and now, for the first time in his life, he feels completely, utterly stuck.
